title: Sleep-like activity in peritumoral brain areas measured with TMS-EEG
summary:
The boundaries between a tumor and healthy parts of the brain are not always easy to identify. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be used to show structural changes in the brain. However, even in structurally intact areas the activity of the brain may be altered. These changes may be related to functional impairments (e.g., motor deficits). They can also potentially serve as risk factors for postoperative deficits.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation is a method of stimulating the cerebral cortex. A magnetic pulse is applied to the brain through the skull bone, triggering a circumscribed current flow on the cortex (= induction current). During this stimulation, the electrical activity of the brain is recorded via an electroencephalogram (EEG). 
This functional testing of the brain could help to uncover differences between healthy brain areas and areas in the immediate vicinity of the tumor. This information could provide new insights into the development of functional deficits due to tumor growth or a surgical intervention and thus also improve preoperative planning.

interventions.name: In patients, 3 stimulation spots (over the tumor, adjacent to the tumor, contralateral) will be stimulated with 150 TMS pulses while an EEG is recorded.
In healthy controls, 2 stimulation spots (over the right and left primary motor cortex) will be stimulated with 150 TMS pulses while an EEG is recorded.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Age above 18 years, Written informed consent; Only patients: Suspected brain tumor after MRI, Participation in TMS measurement
Exclusion criteria:
Contraindications for receiving an MRI, Contraindications for receiving a TMS measurement, More than one generalized seizure per week, Pregnancy, Missing conset to participate in the study; Only healthy controls: History of psychiatric or neurological diseases
